text: Estimation of Chimpanzee Community Size and Genetic Diversity in Kahuzi-Biega National Park, Democratic Republic of Congo

A small chimpanzee habitat in the montane forest of Kahuzi-Biega National Park, Democratic Republic of Congo, is connected with the lowland forest of this park through a corridor, which is affected by human encroachment. To assess the conservation status of the chimpanzee population in this small habitat, we estimated the size of the community and evaluated its genetic diversity by using 279 fecal samples collected in the montane forest of Kahuzi. Using autosomal microsatellite (or short tandem repeat, STR) loci, we identified 32 individuals, comprising 19 females and 13 males. Samples from 24 individuals were collected at least twice and a genetic mark-recapture analysis estimated that the community size was 36 (range: 32-42). Data on nest site sharing confirmed that all the samples belonged to the same community. Nest site sharing information may be useful in population studies of unhabituated chimpanzees. The genetic structure and diversity of the 32 genotyped individuals was assessed using Y-chromosomal short tandem repeat (Y-STR) loci and mitochondrial D-loops. One dominant Y-STR haplotype was found, whereas there was no dominant haplotype in the mitochondrial region, reflecting a female-biased dispersal pattern, which is typical of chimpanzees. The genetic diversity for three markers in Kahuzi chimpanzees was comparable to that in other eastern chimpanzee populations. A relatively high heterozygosity and negative inbreeding coefficient (F IS ) for STR loci suggests that the study community belongs to an outbreeding chimpanzee population. These findings suggest that individuals of the study community may have reproductive contact with other chimpanzee individuals from neighboring communities in Kahuzi-Biega National Park, at least in the recent past.

Wild animal populations are threatened by habitat fragmentation and poaching, which can reduce both the sizes of the populations and their genetic diversity [Janecka et al., 2014;Mondol et al., 2013;Rivera-Ort ız et al., in press]. Chimpanzees are particularly vulnerable to such threats due to their slow reproduction [Nishida et al., 2003]. Human disturbance has a negative effect on chimpanzee populations [Tutin & Fernandez, 1984] and their habitats have decreased [Inskipp, 2005;Junker et al., 2012]. The eastern chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) is found in seven African countries, namely, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Central African Republic, South Sudan, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, and Tanzania [Inskipp, 2005]. The DRC has the majority of the population [Inskipp, 2005] and it is important to study their conservation status in this country.
Estimating the size of a chimpanzee population is one of the most important pieces of information for monitoring the current conservation status. Traditional chimpanzee census methods are based on evaluating indirect signs such as counting their nests along line transects [e.g. Plumptre & Cox, 2006]; however, these methods are often associated with very large confidence intervals that translate into high percentages of the total count. This lack of precision is especially problematic when the goal is to estimate population sizes for small populations of endangered species [Guschanski et al., 2009]. However, advances in genetic techniques have made it possible to capture an individual's DNA from fecal samples rather than the individual itself [Taberlet & Luikart, 1999]. Genetic census using feces can provide accurate and reliable population size estimates [e.g. Kohn et al., 1999]. Collecting scat to identify individuals and estimate population numbers was first used on coyotes [Kohn et al., 1999] and has been used to study great apes: gorillas [Arandjelovic et al., 2010;Gray et al., 2013;Guschanski et al., 2009] and chimpanzees [Arandjelovic et al., 2011;Chancellor et al., 2012;Moore & Vigilant, 2014a]. The genetic census approach appears to be one of the best ways to accurately estimate population sizes.
Genetic diversity is also an important factor for conservation status. Thus, analysis of the genetic structure of a population can provide information that is essential to the conservation of the population or species [Bergle & Vigilant, 2007]. Sex-biased dispersal patterns affect the population genetic structure [Eriksson et al., 2006;Langergraber et al., 2007]. Chimpanzees are a male philopatric species, that is, the males tend to remain in their natal group, while females typically disperse from the natal group at sexual maturity [Nishida & Kawanaka, 1972;Pusey, 1979;Wrangham, 1979]. This behavioral and dispersal pattern affects the genetic variation in the Y-chromosome and in the mitochondria in chimpanzees [Langergraber et al., 2007] and bonobos [Eriksson et al., 2006]. Analyses of several genetic markers may, therefore, enable an accurate estimation of genetic diversity in a chimpanzee population.
In this study, we conducted a genetic analysis of a chimpanzee population in Kahuzi-Biega National park, DRC. In Kahuzi, long-term studies of eastern chimpanzees and Grauer's gorillas (Gorilla beringei graueri) have been conducted [Yamagiwa et al., 1992[Yamagiwa et al., ,2012]]. Yamagiwa et al. [1992] estimated, based on nest counts, that a small population of chimpanzees, comprising at least three relatively small communities, inhabited the montane forest of Kahuzi-Biega at a low density (0.13 individuals per km 2 ). However, in recent years, several armed militia groups have been operating inside the park and have carried out hunting, mining, and farming activities that have degraded habitats and affected animal biodiversity, including the chimpanzee [Hollestelle et al., 2012]. Although it is important to determine the current size of the chimpanzee community, it is difficult to achieve this without complete habituation. The civil war caused sustained poaching in the area that killed half of the gorilla population, including most of the individuals, such as silverbacks, in groups that had been habituated for tourism and research [Yamagiwa, 2003]. Therefore, research programs that avoid habituation are preferable from the conservation perspective at Kahuzi; instead, researchers make use of indirect approaches such as counting nests or analyzing feces. In Kahuzi, fresh chimpanzee nests can easily be found [Basabose & Yamagiwa, 2002] and fresh fecal samples can be collected. Here, we used a genetic mark-recapture approach on fecal samples to estimate the size of one chimpanzee community (Kaboko community) inhabiting the montane forest of Kahuzi. The aim of this study was to determine the size of this community in the Kahuzi-Biega National Park and to estimate its genetic diversity using noninvasive fecal samples. We estimated genetic variation in this community by analyses of autosomal microsatellites (or short tandem repeats, STRs), Y-chromosomal short tandem repeats (Y-STRs), and mtDNA D-loop sequences and compared the level of variation with that of other wild eastern chimpanzee societies. This information may enable us to monitor the changes over time in Kahuzi chimpanzee population dynamics and genetic diversity.

Kahuzi-Biega is one of the largest national parks of the DRC with an area of 6,000 km 2 . It is divided into two sectors: a lowland sector of approximately 5,400 km 2 , ranging at an altitude between 600 and 1,800 m and covered with lowland moist evergreen forest; and a highland sector of approximately 600 km 2 , with an altitude of 1,800-3,308 m and covered with montane forest. The montane forest is connected to the lowland rain forest through a narrow ecological corridor that is 20 km long and 4 km wide (Fig. 1). This ecological corridor has been permanently encroached upon by illegal farming and ore mining [Yamagiwa et al., 2012], resulting in severe habitat disturbance, which may prevent chimpanzees from moving freely between the two forest blocks.
The study area spreads over approximately 80 km 2 of montane forest along the eastern edge of the highland sector of Kahuzi-Biega at an altitude of 2,050-2,350 m above the sea level (Fig. 1).

The Kaboko chimpanzee community in the highland sector of Kahuzi-Biega National Park has been under continuous study since 1994 without complete habituation [Basabose, 2002[Basabose, , 2004[Basabose, , 2005;;Basabose & Yamagiwa, 1997, 2002].
Based on individual identification during daily monitoring, Basabose [2005] counted 23 individuals, including eight adult and adolescent males, seven adult and adolescent females, and eight immature individuals including three infants, which was assumed to constitute the Kaboko community. Recently, two newborn infants were observed within the community, bringing the estimated population to 25 individuals at the time of beginning this research [Basabose, unpublished data].

This research adheres to the American Society of Primatologists (ASP) Principles for Ethical Treatment of Non-human Primates. The study complies with the protocols of the National Strategy for the Conservation of Biodiversity in protected areas in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which is an integral part of the Act No. 11/009 of July 9, 2011 establishing fundamental principles for environment protection in DRC. The study was conducted under the framework of the existing long-term formal collaboration between two Congolese public institutions (the Centre de Recherche en Sciences Naturelles de Lwiro and Kahuzi-Biega National Park).

Chimpanzee fecal samples were collected in the study area (Fig. 1). Samples were only obtained from nest sites encountered opportunistically when routinely tracking fresh chimpanzee trails between October 2011 and June 2013. At all nest sites, only feces estimated to be 1-2 days old were sampled. Only tree nests confirmed to have been used by chimpanzees (presence of fresh feces) were sampled and only fecal samples found in or beneath a night tree nest were collected. One fresh fecal sample per nest was collected at each nest site. However, fresh smaller dung found within the nest of an older individual (based on larger feces diameter) was sampled separately and recorded as presumptive feces from an unweaned infant who might have shared the nest with the mother.
The surface of the feces was scraped and placed in 2 mL of lysis buffer containing 0.5% SDS, 100 mM EDTA (pH 8.0), 100 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), and 10 mM NaCl before extracting DNA [Hayaishi & Kawamoto, 2006]. In total, 279 fecal samples were collected at 51 different nest sites. The geographic coordinates of each sampled nest site were recorded using a Garmin GPS unit for mapping the nest site locations (Fig. 1).

section: dna extraction, sex genotyping, and individual identification
text:
We extracted genomic DNA from the fecal samples using the QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen, Tokyo, Japan) according to the protocol provided by the manufacturer with minor modifications. DNA extracted from noninvasive samples, and especially from fecal samples, is typically degraded and at a low concentration [Inoue et al., 2007;Morin et al., 2001;Taberlet et al., 1996]. To ensure accurate genotyping, we quantified the amount of DNA per sample using a Thermal Cycler Dice Real Time System (TaKaRa, Shiga, Japan) as described by Inoue et al. [2007]. Only samples with >100 pg/mL of DNA were used because allelic dropout rarely happens when using such templates for autosomal microsatellite analysis [Inoue et al., 2007;Morin et al., 2001].
To confirm the sex of an individual, two to four independent PCR amplifications were performed for a segment of the amelogenin locus, which is located in the X-Y homologous region and checked by capillary electrophoresis [Bradley et al., 2001]. Am. J. Primatol.
We prepared three primer sets for 17 STR markers [Arandjelovic et al., 2011;Bradley et al., 2000;Inoue et al., 2008]: set 1 (D16s2624, D5s1457, D5s1470, D1s2130, D18s851, D12s66, and D4s1627); set 2 (D7s817, D1s550, D10s1432, D14s306 , andD8s1106); andset 3 (D2s1329, D11s2002, D9s910,  D3s2459, andD6s1056) as shown in Table I. PCR amplification of each DNA extract was carried out in 5 mL reactions containing 200 nM of each primer, 2.5 mL of QIAGEN Multiplex PCR Master Mix (Qiagen), and 2 mL of DNA template. After an initial incubation at 95°C for 15 min, PCR amplification was performed for 45 cycles consisting of denaturation at 94°C for 30 s, annealing at 57°C for 30 s, and extension at 72°C for 30 s, and a final extension at 60°C for 30 min. The amplification products were separated by capillary electrophoresis using an ABI 3130xl genetic analyzer (Applied Biosystems, Forest City, CA). Allele sizes were manually determined using Peak Scanner Software v1.0 (Applied Biosystems). Samples with any ambiguous results were excluded from the analysis as a conservative measure to avoid any case of contamination that might have happened before and/or during data collection in the field. Inoue et al. (2007) found a 3% allelic dropout rate for extracts containing >100 pg/mL DNA and we used this rate to calculate the number of repetitions necessary to correctly determine homozygous genotypes with 99% certainty. Using this approach, two replications (0.03) 2 were found to be sufficient for samples with more than 100 pg/mL DNA template. As a precaution, we assigned a sample as homozygous at any STR locus if the same allele was exclusively seen in at least three replicate PCRs, and as heterozygous if seen in at least two replicates.
To discriminate individuals, we performed at least three independent PCR amplifications of all samples that contained >100 pg DNA using primer set 1. Using GenAlEx v6.41 [Peakall & Smouse, 2006], we calculated the probability of identity between sibs (PIsibs) [Waits et al., 2001] in order to evaluate whether primer set 1 was adequate for individual discrimination between close relatives. The number of matched and mismatched loci among all genotypes was calculated using CERVUS software [Marshall et al., 1998]. Genotypes from different samples that mismatched at one or two loci were re-examined for possible genotyping errors and in some samples (see results in detail) additional genotyping using primer set 2 was undertaken to resolve any ambiguities. We performed one independent PCR with all the other samples using primer set 2 to confirm the identification from primer set 1. We then assigned a consensus ID to each genotype.
In order to evaluate genetic diversity, we picked one sample for each consensus ID and performed at least three independent PCRs using primer sets 2 and 3. The number of alleles (Na), expected and observed heterozygosities (H E and H O ), inbreeding coefficient (F IS ), and deviations from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) were calculated using GenAlEx.
The community size was estimated using a genetic mark-recapture model that assumed a closed population and utilized individual genotypes collected from one or more nest sites. Before estimating community size, we checked that all samples were derived from the same community using a nest network analysis. We assumed that samples collected from the same nest site were from the same community. The network was constructed from data on nest site sharing using UCINET 6 [Borgatti et al., 2002]. This analysis can reveal whether all collected samples are derived from the same community.
Capwire software [Miller et al., 2005] was used to estimate population size with the two-innate rate method (TIRM). We calculated 95% confidence intervals (CIs). TIRM has previously been assumed in similar studies to be a conservative estimator [Arandjelovic et al., 2010[Arandjelovic et al., , 2011;;Puechmaille & Petit, 2007].

We analyzed 11 Y-STR loci in all 13 males [Erler et al., 2004;Eriksson et al., 2006;Gusmão et al., 2002;Langergraber et al., 2007]. Two Y-STR primer sets were prepared: set 1 with a mix of six primers (DYs439, DYs469, DYs533, DYs 562, DYs632, and DYs520) and set 2 with a mix of five primers (DYs588, DYs510, DYs517, DYs612, and DYs630). Three to four PCRs were performed and genotyping procedures were the same as that for autosomal STR loci.

A 455-base pair segment of the mitochondrial hypervariable control (D-loop) region was amplified with PCR using L16041 (5 0 -CTCTGTTCTTTCAT GGGGAAGC-3 0 ) as the forward primer and H16498 (5 0 -CCTGAAGTAGGAACCAGATG-3 0 ) as the reverse primer [Eriksson et al., 2004;Morin et al., 1994]. PCR amplification was carried out in reaction volumes of 15 mL containing a mixture of 150 mM of each dNTP, 200 nM of each primer, 0.5 U Expand High Fidelity enzyme mix (Expand High Fidelity PCR Systems, Roche Diagnostics K.K., Tokyo, Japan), 0.2 mL of T4 gene 32 protein (Nippon Gene, Tokyo, Japan), and 2 mL of template DNA. After an initial incubation at 95°C for 5 min, PCR amplification was performed for 45 cycles consisting of denaturation at 94°C for 30 s, annealing at 50°C for 30 s, and extension at 72°C for 30 s, and a final extension at 72°C for 30 min. The PCR products were purified using ExoSAP-IT (USB Corporation, Cleveland, OH), sequenced using a Big Dye Terminator ver. 3.1 cycle sequencing kit (Applied Biosystems), and then electrophoresed on an Applied Biosystems 3130xl Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems). Accession numbers for the mitochondrial sequences are AB924650-AB924658 in the DNA Data Bank of Japan (DDBJ).

section: comparison of genetic diversity in eastern chimpanzee populations
text: We used Arlequin 3.5.1.2 [Excoffier & Lischer, 2010] to calculate both Y-STR and mtDNA D-loop haplotype diversity [H; Nei, 1987]. We also compared diversity in mtDNA D-loops and Y-STRs of the eastern chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) populations from four communities in Uganda [Langergraber et al., 2007] and Mahale, Tanzania [Inoue et al., 2013;Inoue, in press]. For Y-STRs, we also included data from Ugalla, Tanzania [Moore & Vigilant, 2014b] and Gishwati, Rwanda [Chancellor et al., 2012]. For STR loci, the number of alleles (Na) and observed heterozygosities (H O ) in this study were compared with the data of Sonso, Uganda [Lukas et al., 2005], Mahale, Tanzania [Inoue et al., 2008], and Ugalla, Tanzania [Moore & Vigilant, 2014b]. We used the four STR loci (D2s1329, D5s1470, D7s817, and D11s2002) that were analyzed in all four regions and compared the averages of the values.

In total, 164 samples successfully yielded genotypes using STR primer set 1. The majority of samples (93.3%) were genotyped at all seven loci and the average proportion of loci genotyped was 0.989. Only five (4.9%) and three (1.8%) samples were genotyped at 6 and 5 loci, respectively. From the 164 samples, we identified 32 individuals, comprising 19 females and 13 males.
In cases where genotypes at all examined loci matched, the number of examined loci was 6 in 56 pairs and 7 in 818 pairs. PIsibs values in these cases were less than 5.0 Â 10 À3 . This implies that it is highly likely that these pairs are derived from the same individuals. The number of examined loci was five or fewer in the other 11 cases, including samples C141, C177, and C248 (Table II). In such cases, the genotype of STR set 2 (as indicated in Table II) was determined with at least three additional independent PCRs and the samples were then confirmed to be derived from the same individuals with low PIsibs values (less than 1.0 Â 10 À3 ).
There were four cases where the genotype of STR set 1 was mismatched at 2 of 6 loci. However, in such cases, the genotype of each sample was heterozygous at the two mismatched loci, implying that these mismatches could not be explained by allelic dropout, which is one of the most common genotyping errors. There was one case with genotype mismatching at 2 of 3 loci (C177 and C248, Table II). We genotyped loci of STR set 2 using those two samples and found four other mismatched loci in STR set 2 (Table II). In all other cases, the number of mismatched loci was three or more. In those cases, the samples are confirmed to be derived from different individuals.
The genotype result from one independent PCR using STR set 2 was investigated to confirm the individual discrimination from STR set 1. In all sample pairs that were determined to be derived from different individuals by STR set 1, two or more mismatched loci were found using STR set 2. In sample pairs determined to be derived from the same individuals by STR set 1, there were no mismatched loci from STR set 2, except for the pairs that included samples C121 and C233. In such pairs, one mismatched locus was found, which could be explained by allelic dropout of C121 at locus D1s550 and of C233 at locus D10s1432. Given that a 3% allelic dropout may apply to our samples, these results suggest that our subsequent analyses based on individual discrimination determined by STR set 1 were reliable.

section: number of individuals in the community
text:
All individuals except one (ID 11) shared at least one nest site, and network analysis based on nest site sharing data showed that all these individuals belonged to the same community (Fig. 2). The fecal sample from ID 11 was found only once in a nest site comprising three nests. Samples from the other two nests within this site had small amounts of DNA (less than 100 pg/mL) and were excluded from the analysis. However, the genotype of one of the excluded samples was determined for 11 of the 12 STR loci (sets 1 and 2) in three independent replicates of the PCR; these genotyped loci gave identical results to individual ID 10 (Fig. 2). If this sample with its small amount of DNA is included in the analysis, then all the genotyped individuals are linked.
The number of individuals detected in the nesting sites varied from one to 12 (mean ¼ 3.6 AE SD 3.2) over the entire sampling period. Throughout the study period, only eight individuals (25%),  Ã For these samples, genotypes of STR set 2 were determined with at least three independent PCR amplifications including the two individuals thought to be infants from their small dung size (diameter <2 cm), were sampled in only one nest site. Using the data on the number of samples, Capwire estimated that the community totaled 36 members (95%CI ¼ 32-42).

Information from 17 STR loci is shown in Table I. With one exception (D10s1432), the loci conformed to the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Expected heterozygosity was high (average: 0.756) and F IS was negative on average.

Only three polymorphic loci were found among the 11 Y-STR loci examined. Five different haplotypes were found among the 13 males; haplotype A was the most common, being present in nine individuals (Fig. 3). Each of the four other haplotypes was present in only one male. Haplotype diversity was estimated as 0.54 AE SD 0.16.

The samples from the 32 identified individuals yielded a total of nine unique mtDNA haplotypes. In contrast to the Y-haplotype, no single haplotype dominated, although nine individuals (28%) shared haplotype F (Fig. 3). MtDNA haplotype diversity was estimated as 0.86 AE SD 0.03.

Reliable estimates of population size are vital for conservation and successful management of wild animals [McKechnie et al., 2007;van Schaik et al., 1995]. We used a non-invasive genetic method in the present study and found that the Kaboko chimpanzee community in the montane forest of Kahuzi-Biega National Park comprised at least 32 individuals (19 females and 13 males). A Capwire analysis produced an estimate of 36 individuals (95%CI ¼ 32-42) for the community. The estimate produced by the genetic census was somewhat higher than that from direct observation (about 25 individuals). The estimate by direct observation without complete habituation may be underestimated because chimpanzees live in fission-fusion society [Nishida, 1968] and it is difficult to observe some peripheral females and their infants [Langergraber et al., 2014a]. For the estimate by genetic analysis, we need to consider that 21 months sampling period might violate the assumption of a closed population for Capwire analysis, and thus the number by genetic estimation might be somewhat overestimated although the rate of birth, mortality, immigration, and emigration is relatively low in chimpanzees [Nishida et al., 2003]. However, in comparison with direct observation, the genetic-based estimate might be presumed to provide a realistic assessment of the population size. Moreover, the genetic estimation method provides a true minimum of the number of individuals during the sampling period as it is based on the number of genotypes present in the samples.
We estimated population size of a chimpanzee community with the two-innate rate model (TIRM) which assume a population comprising two groups of individuals with distinct capture probabilities [Miller et al., 2005]. Inoue et al. [2007] reported that it is difficult to collect fecal samples from infant chimpanzees even when following habituated chimpanzees. Our result is consistent with this report. We genotyped two very small dung samples (diameter <2 cm) in our study and consider these individuals to be infants. Samples from these two individuals were encountered only once during the study period. It is also expected to have less chance to collect the samples from some peripheral females [Langergraber et al., 2014a]. These suggest sampling bias in chimpanzee population. Therefore, TIRM might be appropriate for estimating population size of chimpanzee communities.
Here, we used a noninvasive genetic markrecapture method, which assumed a closed population, to estimate with high accuracy the population size of a group-living species. For this approach to be successful, it may be important to consider the group to which genotyped individuals belong. Previous noninvasive genetic studies on chimpanzees were unable to confirm reliably that all collected samples were from individuals belonging to the same community. In a study on chimpanzee populations in Gabon, Arandjelovic et al. [2011] estimated community identity from Y-STR haplotypes and the location of the samples. Although a pattern of male philopatry and female-biased dispersal can enable assignment of an individual to a community on the basis of Y-STRs, there are limitations to this method in some populations. For example, there are normally several Y-STR haplotypes in one community, but some haplotypes are found in only a few males [Langergraber et al., 2007; this study]. In addition, previous studies have observed the transfer of a young male chimpanzee of about 5 years old with his mother in Mahale [Nishida et al., 1985;Takahata & Takahata, 1989]. Y-chromosome haplotype sharing between neighboring chimpanzee communities has been confirmed in Budongo Forest Reserve, Uganda [Langergraber et al., 2014b] and Mahale chimpanzee communities [Inoue, in press]. Consequently, shared Y-STRs may occur between neighboring chimpanzee communities, albeit rarely. These factors indicate the need for some caution when relying on Y-STR haplotypes to define a community.
In the present study, we used information on nest site sharing to identify the community. The nest site sharing analysis showed that all the genotyped individuals are linked if one sample with its small amount of DNA is included in the analysis. This suggests that the identified individuals are members of the same community and this probably leads to the narrow 95%CI of our estimate.

section: genetic diversity of kahuzi chimpanzees and conservation implications
text:
We found high diversity in mtDNAs and low diversity of Y-chromosome haplotypes. One Y-chromosome haplotype was dominant in the Kaboko community, whereas no dominant haplotype was found for mitochondrial DNA. These results likely reflect male philopatry and female-biased dispersal patterns similar to other chimpanzee communities [Boesch & Boesch-Achermann, 2000;Goodall, 1986;Nishida et al., 1990].
Despite the minor differences observed between sites, Kahuzi chimpanzees have similar genetic diversity as other eastern chimpanzee populations (Table III). Although Y-STR diversity in Kahuzi chimpanzees was slightly lower than the average Y-STR diversity calculated for four chimpanzee communities in Uganda (Table III), the diversity in mitochondrial and autosomal microsatellites is still important for conservation of chimpanzees given that the communities have female-biased dispersal patterns. On the basis of mitochondrial D-loop and autosomal microsatellites, Kahuzi chimpanzees show comparable genetic diversity to their conspecific populations (Table III).
Although the corridor connecting highland and lowland sectors in Kahuzi has been continuously encroached upon in the last three decades by farmers and illegal ore mining concessionaires, the chimpanzees inhabiting the highland sector of Kahuzi-Biega National Park showed a high observed heterozygosity (H O ) and a negative inbreeding coefficient (F IS ). This suggests that the Kaboko community belongs to an outbreeding population. Female chimpanzees in the highland sector may have probably been transferred between communities. Moreover, previous genetic analyses suggested that gorillas may have traversed the corridor and entered into reproductive contact with the gorilla population ranging the lowland sector [Saltonstall et al., 1998]. The genetic diversity results found in this study might reflect the fact that the chimpanzee populations in the highland and lowland sectors have been in reproductive contact in the recent past, in a similar manner as the sympatric gorilla populations. This expectation is consistent with reports that a large part of the corridor that was untouched by poacherswas still used by gorillas and chimpanzees, as evidenced by the observation of their fresh nests prior to large-scale deforestation [Refisch, 1991]. In the Bossou chimpanzee community, where female immigration from other communities is limited, it has been reported that one mitochondrial haplotype is dominant and that the risk of losing mitochondrial diversity is high [Shimada et al., 2009]. Likewise, a chimpanzee population inhabiting the easternmost distribution of the chimpanzee range in dry and open habitat in Ugalla shows extremely low Y-chromosome haplotype diversity [Moore & Vigilant, 2014b] in comparison to other chimpanzee communities (Table III). It has been suggested that this low Ychromosome haplotype diversity could be the first indication of isolation and loss of genetic diversity in this population [Moore & Vigilant, 2014b]. In Kahuzi, genetic diversity is still relatively high and the status of the population is less threatened compared to Bossou and Ugalla chimpanzee populations. However, there has been extensive human activity in the corridor in Kahuzi. In the 1950s, villages were evacuated from the deep forest, but a few human settlements remain within the lowland sector near the park's corridor. Much of the Kahuzi corridor habitat has been subjected to large-scale and lowtechnology ore mining and timber cutting activities since the 1980s [Hall et al., 1998]. Recently, rampant deforestation due to illegal timber cutting, mineral mining, and cutting for agricultural fields has affected about 80% of the corridor, disturbing the movement of large forest dwelling mammals, including elephants and great apes, in and around the corridor. If the current ecological corridor becomes completely deforested, the small isolated chimpanzee population inhabiting the highland sector of Kahuzi will be highly susceptible to inbreeding in the short term and may suffer a limited evolutionary development [Keller & Waller, 2002;Lacy, 1997]. To ensure the long-term survival of Kahuzi chimpanzees, conservation efforts need to focus on restoring the ecological corridor connecting the highland and lowland sectors of the Kahuzi-Biega National Park. Such an effort would enable the continuation of regular reproductive contacts between the chimpanzee populations in the montane and lowland forests and, thereby, preserve viable genetic diversity in both populations.
More genetic studies are needed on the chimpanzee communities adjacent to the Kaboko community and on the chimpanzee population inhabiting the lowland sector of the park to get a more holistic understanding of the genetic structure of chimpanzee populations in the Kahuzi-Biega National Park.
